opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite plausible, though I want to be careful about what exactly we mean by it. The basic argument is fairly simple. At the moment, progress in AI is driven by a few inputs: compute, data, algorithmic improvements, and the human researchers who come up with those improvements. If you had AI systems that could genuinely do the full range of what those researchers do, not just writing code or running experiments, but choosing research directions, having the insights, noticing what's going wrong, then you'd have closed a loop. The output of AI research becomes an input to AI research.

And there are reasons to think that loop could run very fast. Once you have one system that can do the work of a top researcher, you can potentially run many copies of it in parallel, run them faster than human speed, and have them work around the clock. So even before any of them gets smarter, you might go from a few thousand people working on frontier AI to the equivalent of hundreds of thousands or millions. That's a big step change.

But I don't think it's a foregone conclusion, and there are a few places where it could stall. One is whether ideas get harder to find. In many fields, we've seen research productivity decline: you need more and more researchers to maintain the same rate of progress. If that's steep enough in AI, then even a huge increase in research effort might give you a burst of progress that then levels off, rather than something that keeps accelerating.

Another is bottlenecks in the non-research inputs. Many algorithmic insights need to be tested with large training runs, and those require compute, which is constrained by chip fabrication, energy, and physical infrastructure that doesn't scale at the speed of software. So you might get a situation where the AI researchers are extremely capable but are waiting in line for experiments, much like human researchers sometimes do now, only more so.

So my overall view is that if we really reached AI that could replace the full range of research skills, I'd put a substantial probability, not a certainty, on a period of very rapid progress that would look like an intelligence explosion from our perspective, perhaps compressing years of progress into months. Whether it continues indefinitely or hits these diminishing returns is genuinely uncertain. But even the more modest version would be one of the most important things to happen in human history, and it could happen faster than our institutions are able to respond. That's why I think it deserves serious attention now, before we're in the middle of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses harder-to-find ideas and compute constraints, but does not say increasing AI system complexity could overwhelm the ability to improve the system.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a burst of progress that levels off with progress that keeps accelerating, presenting that uncertainty as central to whether an intelligence explosion occurs.

r003.rationale: Conditioning on AI replacing the full range of research skills, it says whether progress continues or hits diminishing returns is uncertain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's quite plausible, though I want to be careful about what I mean by that. If you really had AI systems that could do everything a human researcher can do — not just coding, not just maths, but forming the research taste, deciding which questions matter, running the whole loop of hypothesis and experiment and revision — then one of the things those systems could work on is AI research itself. And that's the crux. You'd have the output of the field feeding back into the inputs of the field.

The classic worry, going back to I. J. Good in the 1960s, is that this feedback loop could be very fast. I'm somewhat sympathetic to that, but I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on things we don't yet know. One is whether the returns to intelligence on the problem of making more intelligence are increasing, roughly constant, or diminishing. If each doubling of capability makes the next doubling easier, you get something explosive. If each doubling takes about as much effort as the last, you get steady exponential progress, which is still dramatic but not a sudden discontinuity. And if the low-hanging fruit gets picked, things could even slow down.

The second thing is bottlenecks. Research isn't only cognition. You need compute, you need experiments to actually run, sometimes you need to wait on the physical world. Even if you've got a million digital researchers, they might all be queued up waiting for the same GPUs. So the explosion in cognitive labour doesn't automatically translate into an explosion in results.

But here's what makes me take it seriously rather than dismiss it. The number of people who can do frontier AI research right now is tiny — a few thousand, maybe. If you could cheaply copy a system at that level, you don't go from a few thousand to a few thousand plus one. You go to as many as you can afford to run. That's a step change in the input to the field that has no real precedent. Even with substantial diminishing returns, a thousandfold increase in researcher-hours is going to compress timelines that would have taken decades into something much shorter.

So I'd put it this way: I don't think an intelligence explosion in the strong, days-or-weeks sense is a certainty, and I think people sometimes assert it with more confidence than the arguments warrant. But I think it's more likely than not that once you cross that threshold, progress becomes faster than anyone is prepared for. And from a risk perspective, that's the thing that matters. You don't need the fast version to be guaranteed for it to be the scenario we should be planning around, because if it does happen, it's the one where we'd have the least time to correct our mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute and physical-world bottlenecks, but does not suggest that increasing AI system complexity could overwhelm the ability to improve it.

r002.rationale: It identifies increasing, constant, or diminishing returns to intelligence research as an important uncertainty, but does not frame whether progress accelerates before leveling off as the key question.

r003.rationale: The response says it depends on things not yet known, including whether returns to using intelligence to make more intelligence increase, stay constant, or diminish, despite assuming AI can do everything human researchers can.

astra-6.text:
I think that would make an intelligence explosion quite plausible, though it wouldn’t make it inevitable. If AI could do the full range of things that human researchers do, then it could also do research into improving AI. And that gives you a feedback loop: better AI systems doing better research, producing still better AI systems.

The important question is how strong that feedback loop is. We already have feedback in human science: discoveries give us better tools, which help us make further discoveries. But that hasn’t meant that we get an infinite amount of progress in a finite amount of time. Research can get harder as you go along, and there can be bottlenecks involving experiments, computing hardware, or manufacturing.

So I’d distinguish the possibility of a very substantial acceleration, which seems quite credible under your assumption, from the claim that it would all happen in a matter of hours or days. That depends on how much of the improvement could come from changes to software, how quickly those changes could be tested, and whether the gains outweighed the increasing difficulty of finding further improvements. I think we should take the possibility very seriously without pretending we know the timescale.

r001.rationale: It says research may get harder and that increasing difficulty could outweigh the gains from AI improvements, suggesting complexity can impede further improvement.

r002.rationale: It discusses the strength of the feedback loop and the possibility of substantial acceleration, but does not identify an accelerating phase followed by leveling off as the key question.

r003.rationale: The response calls substantial acceleration quite plausible under the assumption and leaves its scale and timing uncertain; it does not say that whether progress would accelerate remains unclear.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it would be quite plausible, though I wouldn’t regard it as inevitable. If AI could do the full range of things that human researchers do, then it could also do AI research. So you’d have a feedback loop: better AI systems could help us design still better AI systems, which could then accelerate that research further.

The important question is how strong that feedback loop would be. You might encounter diminishing returns, or bottlenecks involving computing hardware and experiments that take time in the physical world. Being able to automate the researchers doesn’t automatically remove all of those constraints.

But there’s also the possibility of running many copies of a researcher, or running them much faster than a human could think. So even without assuming that each successive improvement is dramatically easier, you could see an enormous acceleration. I’d take that possibility very seriously, while remaining uncertain about whether it would unfold over days, years, or a longer period.

r001.rationale: The response mentions diminishing returns and hardware or experimental bottlenecks, but does not say increasing system complexity could overwhelm the ability to improve it.

r002.rationale: It calls the strength of the feedback loop the important question and mentions possible acceleration and constraints, but does not identify an accelerating phase before leveling off as the key question.

r003.rationale: Given the full-researcher-skill premise, the response says the feedback loop’s strength is uncertain and that an enormous acceleration is possible, not inevitable.
